tier_reason: The nuster wiki page (a competitor's author) publishes wrk commands, server configs, versions and the CPU (Xeon X5650) but no compiler or flags (distribution packages) and no harness repo; it is neither first-party to Varnish nor peer reviewed, so C. On equal resources (nginx worker_processes auto on 12 cores) nginx proxy_cache beats Varnish in all 18 rows of the three tables; the only Varnish wins are against a single nginx worker.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Not faster on equal footing. Table 1 (1 Gbps, 1000 connections), requests/s: hello-world 12 B Varnish 133094 vs nginx 1 worker 33454 (3.98x, derived from page data) but vs nginx 12 workers 214217 (0.62x, derived from page data); 1 KB Varnish 87772 vs nginx 1 worker 36034 (2.44x, derived from page data) and vs nginx 12 workers 91497 (0.96x, derived from page data). Table 2 (loopback, 1000 connections) hello-world: Varnish 115928 vs nginx 1 worker 30996 (3.74x, derived from page data) and vs nginx 12 workers 136844 (0.85x, derived from page data). Table 3 (loopback, 5000 connections) hello-world: Varnish 111711 vs nginx 12 workers 125309 (0.89x, derived from page data); nginx 1 worker is marked ERROR in every Table 3 row. nginx with all cores beats Varnish in every row of all three tables. No number against an origin server without a cache was found, and Varnish publishes no figures in its README.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars, 391 forks; widely deployed HTTP accelerator
corrections.caveats: The only numeric comparison found is a competitor's wiki page (nuster author; nuster tops every table), page last edited 13 Aug 2018 with sample-output Date headers of 5 Nov 2017, on old releases (Varnish 4.1.8, nginx 1.12.2, wrk with --timeout 300 and -t 100); not a first-party Varnish claim and not peer reviewed, so tier C. The only wins are against a single nginx worker (an asymmetric baseline against multi-threaded Varnish); nginx on 12 workers beats Varnish in every row, and Varnish logged socket timeouts in two rows (17 at 1 KB in Table 1, 118 at hello-world in Table 2). Varnish's thread settings were left at defaults. The origin-without-cache baseline in the assignment has no number anywhere reachable (a varnish/hitch issue reports about 10,835 req/s through Varnish against 776 req/s through a TLS path, which is not an origin comparison). The GitHub repository was archived on 2026-02-16 (last commit 'Moving') and its README says development moved to code.vinyl-cache.org with the last usable GitHub version tagged 'last' (that site did not resolve from this container, so it was not checked); maintenance_status is 'unknown' for that reason. Related prior work: the AdaptSize paper tunes Varnish admission and reports hit-ratio gains over stock Varnish, which is not a comparison against Varnish as the winner.

notes: All table numbers on the nuster wiki match the record; derived ratios recomputed and correct. Rejected as not-faster against the equal-resource baseline (nginx proxy_cache with all cores); keep with a 'not faster' shortcoming if policy keeps it. Archived repo, development moved to Vinyl Cache (unreachable), so maintenance left 'unknown' rather than 'abandoned'.

tier_reason: Vendor-run cassandra-stress comparison (ScyllaDB 4.4 vs Cassandra 4.0) with no public harness, compiler or CPU model; the vendor page and white paper did not resolve (ENOTFOUND), but a fresh WebSearch repeated the 3x-8x and 2.66x-8x figures, so first-party, snippet-only C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Vendor claim (search-result text only, page not opened): 3x-8x the throughput of Cassandra 4.0 on identical 3-node i3.4xlarge clusters at P99 under 10 ms (white-paper table: about 3x at P90 under 10 ms, 2.66x-8x at P99 under 10 ms); in the '4 vs 40' test, 4 ScyllaDB i3.metal nodes give 33% more throughput than 40 Cassandra i3.4xlarge nodes at P99 under 10 ms in one vendor statement and 42% more for a 40 TB cluster that costs 2.5x less in another; the vendor's '80% to 2,200% higher Cassandra P99' figure was not seen again in this check; a New Stack summary of the same tests gives 2x to 4.5x (not re-checked). The repository README only claims 'order-of-magnitude performance improvements' with no figures.
corrections.hardware: AWS i3.4xlarge (3-node clusters, 48 vCPUs in total) and i3.metal (4 ScyllaDB nodes) against 40 x i3.4xlarge for Cassandra (about 2.5x the vCPUs of the ScyllaDB cluster), per search-result text; CPU model and OS tuning not seen.

notes: scylladb.com, www.scylladb.com and the white-paper PDF all ENOTFOUND; numbers rest on search snippets that agree across two independent queries. Seed assignment baseline is Apache Cassandra, so baseline_in_list true stands; category columnar-analytics fits poorly (wide-column OLTP store). License file confirmed as ScyllaDB Software License Agreement v1.1 (non-OSI), so 'reference' stands.

tier_reason: The vendor forum post (2017 YCSB vs Cassandra 3.11.1) did not resolve, and a fresh search confirmed only its setup and a directional throughput lead, not the per-workload figures; the only opened, public-code benchmark (MaibornWolff/database-performance-comparison) shows YugabyteDB slower than the assigned single-node PostgreSQL baseline and slower than Cassandra.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Not faster than the assigned baseline. Independent public-code benchmark (MaibornWolff/database-performance-comparison, YugabyteDB 2.15.0 on 3 x i3.8xlarge, 8 cores and 10 GB per database node): YSQL 295,000 inserts/s vs single-instance PostgreSQL 428,000 (0.69x, derived from page data); YCQL 288,000 vs Cassandra 389,000 sync and 410,000 async (0.74x and 0.70x, derived from page data); YSQL query times 160 s vs 39 s (count-events) and 1700 s vs 119 s (temperature-stats-per-device), newest-per-device failed on YSQL. Vendor claim against Cassandra 3.11.1 (2017, search-result text only, page not opened, per-workload figures not corroborated by a second search): workload A about 74,710 ops/s for Cassandra vs 90,520 for YugaByte DB (1.21x) and workload C about 72,873 vs 103,484 (1.42x); on the 100% read workload about 42% faster at 1 million keys and 95% faster at 10 million keys; a later vendor post says YugabyteDB 1.1 averages more than 2.5x Cassandra 3.11 at 10M keys.
corrections.hardware: Vendor 2017 test: 3 Google Compute n1-standard-16 nodes (16 vCPUs, 60 GB RAM, 2 x 375 GB SSD each), replication factor 3, per search-result text; CPU model not seen.
corrections.workload: Vendor 2017 YCSB comparison of YugaByte DB's Cassandra-compatible YCQL API against Apache Cassandra 3.11.1 on identical 3-node clusters (replication factor 3, consistency levels chosen so both are strongly consistent) at 1, 5 and 10 million keys, using a YCSB fork with an enhanced prepared-statement Cassandra binding.
corrections.license: Apache-2.0 (core database: src/, java/, python/ and build tooling) AND LicenseRef-PolyForm-Free-Trial-1.0.0 (YugabyteDB Anywhere: managed/, troubleshoot/)
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: forum.yugabyte.com, yugabyte.com and docs.yugabyte.com did not resolve from this container (ENOTFOUND), so the vendor figures come from one WebSearch result summary and were not corroborated; a second verifier search confirmed only the setup (3 x n1-standard-16, RF 3, Cassandra 3.11.1, 1/5/10 million keys) and a throughput and p99 lead that grows with key count. Vendor-run, 2017, Cassandra 3.11.1, with a YCSB fork whose Cassandra binding the vendor modified, and a Cassandra configuration retuned by the vendor (G1GC, 12 GB heap) in the follow-up post. Opposite independent evidence was opened: MaibornWolff/database-performance-comparison (Apache-2.0, YugabyteDB 2.15.0 on 3 x i3.8xlarge, IoT insert workload) reports YSQL 295,000 inserts/s against single-instance PostgreSQL 428,000, YCQL 288,000 against Cassandra 389,000 (sync) and 410,000 (async), and YSQL query times 160 s vs 39 s (count-events), 1700 s vs 119 s (temperature-stats-per-device), with newest-per-device failing; so YugabyteDB is slower than both assigned and Cassandra baselines there (3-node YugabyteDB against single-instance PostgreSQL, which also carries replication cost). The repo's own docs (docs/content/stable/benchmark/, faq/comparisons/cassandra.md and postgresql.md) give YugabyteDB-only numbers or qualitative comparisons, with no head-to-head figures; README says only 'high-performance' and 'PostgreSQL-like performance' for the cost-based optimizer. The repository is dual-licensed: the database is Apache-2.0 but YugabyteDB Anywhere (managed/) is under the non-OSI PolyForm Free Trial License 1.0.0. Search snippets also mention user issues reporting YSQL far slower than PostgreSQL on single-node workloads (snippet only).

notes: Rejected as not-faster against the assigned single-node PostgreSQL baseline (and against Cassandra in the only opened independent benchmark); the 2017 vendor Cassandra win stays snippet-only. Keep with a 'not faster' shortcoming if policy keeps it; license corrected to dual Apache-2.0 / PolyForm Free Trial, usability mixed.
